whyItExists.problem: Programs crash when unexpected things happen — a file that doesn't exist, a network timeout, invalid user input. Letting errors propagate as unhandled exceptions gives users a bad experience.
whyItExists.solution: try/except lets you catch and handle errors gracefully. You can give users a helpful message, retry the operation, or log the error and continue.
whyItExists.whenToUse: At program boundaries — user input, file I/O, network calls. Where failure is expected and handleable. When you want to clean up resources regardless of success/failure.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: Don't catch exceptions you can't handle. Don't use bare except: — it catches everything including KeyboardInterrupt. Prefer LBYL (Look Before You Leap) when the check is cheap: if key in dict rather than try: dict[key].

explainModes.beginner: When Python encounters an error (like dividing by zero), it raises an exception. If you don't catch it, the program crashes. try/except lets you say: 'Try this code, and if this specific error happens, do this instead.'
explainModes.simple: try: ... except ErrorType: ... else: ... finally: ... except runs only if the error occurred. else runs only if NO error occurred. finally ALWAYS runs — good for cleanup. raise ErrorType('message') to create your own error. raise alone inside except re-raises the same error.
explainModes.standard: Exception hierarchy: BaseException → Exception → (ValueError, TypeError, KeyError, ...). Catch specific exceptions — catching Exception is already broad. Multiple excepts: except (TypeError, ValueError) as e: — catch either. as e gives you the exception object. e.args for the message. traceback module for detailed stack traces. Context managers (__exit__) integrate with exception handling.
explainModes.technical: Python exceptions are classes — raise RuntimeError('msg') creates a RuntimeError instance. except clause does isinstance check. Exception chaining: raise NewError('msg') from original preserves the original traceback. Suppressing: from contextlib import suppress; with suppress(FileNotFoundError): — clean alternative to try/except/pass. sys.exc_info() inside except gives (type, value, traceback). warnings.warn() for non-fatal issues.
explainModes.deepDive: Exception groups (Python 3.11+): ExceptionGroup for handling multiple exceptions from concurrent tasks. try*: block (Python 3.11+) to match exceptions from a group. The traceback module: traceback.format_exc() for string representation. logging.exception() logs at ERROR level AND includes the traceback. sys.excepthook for global unhandled exception handler. ThreadingError vs asyncio exception handling patterns.

items: ValueError — right type, wrong value: int('abc'), math.sqrt(-1)
KeyError — dict key doesn't exist: d['missing']
IndexError — list index out of range: lst[99]
AttributeError — object doesn't have that attribute: None.strip()

questions.question: When does the 'else' block in a try/except/else run?
options: Always, as a fallback when there is no except
Only when an exception WAS caught
Only when NO exception occurred in the try block
It is the same as finally
questions.explanation: The else block runs only when the try block completed without raising any exception. It's the 'happy path' code — separate from the try block to make the intent clear: 'I expect this to succeed, and if it does, do this.' The finally block runs regardless of whether an exception occurred.

faq.q: Should I catch Exception or be more specific?
faq.a: Be specific. Catching Exception is too broad — it hides programming errors (bugs). Catching the most specific exception you can handle makes your error handling intentional. If you do catch Exception, always log it: logging.exception('Unexpected error') — this preserves the stack trace.

raise NewError('message') from original_error creates exception chaining — the new error's __cause__ points to the original. Python displays both when showing the traceback. Use it when translating low-level errors to higher-level ones: raise HTTPError('Request failed') from connection_error.
